hints: List the three ionisable groups in lysine, two $\text{-NH}_{2}$ groups and one $\text{-COOH}$ group, and remember low pH favours protonated $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COOH}$, high pH favours $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$.
Recall that at the isoelectric point the overall charge is zero, so think what combination of $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$, $\text{-NH}_{2}$, $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ gives net zero for lysine.
walkthrough:
Picture lysine as three acid base switches**
Think of lysine as $\text{H}_{2}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$ in its fully neutral form. Each $\text{-NH}_{2}$ can pick up $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ in acid, and the $\text{-COOH}$ can lose $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{-COO}^{-}$ in base. pH simply sets the position of these equilibria.

Build the low pH and isoelectric forms**
At pH 7.00, which is well below the isoelectric point of 9.47, the molecule is protonated relative to the neutral zwitterion and carries a net positive charge: $^{+}\text{H}_{3}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$. At pH 9.47 the positive and negative charges exactly balance to give net zero, the $\text{-COOH}$ has deprotonated but the side chain $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ remains protonated: $^{+}\text{H}_{3}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COO}^{-}$.

Build the high pH form**
At pH 12.00, well above all $\text{p}K_{a}$ values of the ammonium groups, both nitrogen atoms are deprotonated to $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and the acid is fully deprotonated. That leaves only the $\text{-COO}^{-}$ charge: $\text{H}_{2}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COO}^{-}$ with net charge -1.

Final answer: lysine at pH 7.00: $^{+}\text{H}_{3}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$, net charge +1
lysine at pH 9.47: $^{+}\text{H}_{3}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COO}^{-}$, net charge 0
lysine at pH 12.00: $\text{H}_{2}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COO}^{-}$, net charge -1

hints: Recall the general reaction of a carboxylic acid with $\text{PCl}_{5}$ and what functional group replaces the $\text{-OH}$ of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$.
Look at tyrosine and count the nucleophilic sites that can attack an acyl chloride, the phenolic $\text{-OH}$, the $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and the $\text{-COOH}$.
Use the clue that E contains an ester linkage and F does not, to decide which site reacts in each isomer.
walkthrough:
Make D, a much better electrophile**
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{PCl}_{5} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} + \text{POCl}_{3} + \text{HCl}$. The $\text{-OH}$ of ethanoic acid is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ to give ethanoyl chloride, D: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C(=O)-Cl}$. Acyl chlorides react readily with even weak nucleophiles without heating.

Form E at the phenol oxygen**
Tyrosine has a phenolic $\text{-OH}$ which can act as a nucleophile toward $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$. Attack of the phenolic oxygen on the carbonyl carbon, followed by loss of $\text{HCl}$, gives the phenyl ester: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-O-}$ linked to the benzene ring, while the $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$ side chain is untouched. This is E, the ester isomer.

Form F at the amine nitrogen**
The primary $\text{-NH}_{2}$ group is an even stronger nucleophile. Attack of nitrogen on $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ gives the amide: $\text{-NH-C(=O)-CH}_{3}$, while the phenol $\text{-OH}$ and carboxylic acid remain unchanged. This is F, $\text{HO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NHCOCH}_{3})\text{COOH}$. E and F are structural isomers with the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}$ group in different positions.

Final answer: D: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$, ethanoyl chloride
E: phenyl ethanoate ester of tyrosine, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$ (para ester, $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ unchanged)
F: amide of tyrosine, $\text{HO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NHCOCH}_{3})\text{COOH}$ (phenol unchanged)

hints: Treat the tyrosine benzene ring as a phenol and recall the activating effect of the $\text{-OH}$ group on electrophilic substitution.
For $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, decide which protons are acidic enough to be removed, compare phenol, carboxylic acid and amine.
For $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$ and concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$, recall how many positions ortho and para to $\text{-OH}$ are available when the para position is already substituted.
walkthrough:
Brominate ortho to the phenol**
The $\text{-OH}$ group strongly activates the ring and directs to 2, 4 and 6 positions. In tyrosine the 4 (para) position is blocked by the $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$ substituent, and you are told to ignore its directing effect. With excess bromine, both available ortho positions react to give the 2,6-dibromo phenol. No catalyst is needed because phenol is so reactive.

Deprotonate with excess alkali**
$\text{NaOH}$ is a base, not an electrophile here. Both the carboxylic acid ($\text{p}K_{a}$ about 2) and the phenol ($\text{p}K_{a}$ about 10) are deprotonated by excess $\text{NaOH}$ to give $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and $\text{-O}^{-}$. The amine remains as $\text{-NH}_{2}$ because $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ is not present in neutral tyrosine and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ is not acidic. The product is the disodium salt with phenoxide and carboxylate groups.

Nitrate ortho to the phenol**
Nitration also follows phenol directing. $\text{HNO}_{3}$ provides the $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ electrophile which substitutes ortho to $\text{-OH}$. With excess reagent, substitution can occur at one or both of the 2 and 6 positions, so a mono nitro product at position 2 (or 6) or the 2,6-dinitro product are both correct. The side chain is unchanged.

Final answer: With excess $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$: 2,6-dibromo product, Br at both positions ortho to the phenolic $\text{-OH}$, side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{COOH}$ unchanged.
With excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$: both $\text{-COOH}$ and phenolic $\text{-OH}$ deprotonated to $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and $\text{-O}^{-}$, $\text{-NH}_{2}$ unchanged.
With excess $\text{HNO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$: nitration ortho to $\text{-OH}$, $\text{-NO}_{2}$ at position 2 or 6, or 2,6-dinitro product accepted.

hints: Remember $R_{f}$ compares how far the spot moves relative to how far the solvent front moves, measured from the same origin line.
walkthrough:
Define the ratio**
Picture the TLC plate with a pencil baseline. After development you measure how far the centre of the amino acid spot has moved up from the baseline, and how far the solvent front has moved up from the same baseline. Then $R_{f} = \frac{\text{distance travelled by solute}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent}}$. It has no units and is always less than 1.
Final answer: $R_{f}$ = distance travelled by amino acid (solute spot) divided by distance travelled by solvent front, both measured from the baseline.

hints: Link a larger $R_{f}$ (0.45 for tyrosine versus 0.14 for lysine) to spending more time in the mobile phase and less time adsorbed on the stationary phase.
walkthrough:
Connect movement to interactions**
A spot only moves when it is dissolved in the moving solvent. When it is adsorbed on the silica stationary phase it stays still. Tyrosine travels further ($R_{f}$ 0.45) than lysine ($R_{f}$ 0.14), so tyrosine must spend a greater fraction of time in the mobile phase. In other words, tyrosine is more soluble in the solvent used, while lysine is more strongly attracted to the polar stationary phase and is held back.

Final answer: Tyrosine has higher $R_{f}$ because it is more soluble in the mobile solvent (less strongly adsorbed on the stationary phase) than lysine, ORA lysine is more attracted to the stationary phase.
